title: From Reusable to Regeneratable: Rethinking the Shared UI Component Library
gist: Argues that coding agents have made regenerating UI components cheaper than maintaining a canonical shared component library, so organizations should centralize the design system, tokens, machine-readable guidelines and tests, verify generated code, and keep only a few hard components (e.g. accessibility-critical) as curated shared code.

insights.claim: Generative coding agents have made regenerating standard UI components cheaper than maintaining one canonical company-wide component library, so the shared library now buys less than it once did.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Platform-team budgets for internal UI libraries are harder to justify; watch for shrinking demand for component-library tooling and maintenance.
insights.locator: Key Takeaways

insights.claim: A shared library bundled four promises (reuse, consistency, encoded expertise, single source of truth); only reuse and encoded expertise require shipped code, and those are the parts AI can now help with.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Use the four-jobs test to decide whether a library earns its cost versus a design system plus tests.
insights.locator: What the Library Was Really For

insights.claim: The expensive part of a shared UI library is the decade of maintenance after the first release, including ownership disputes, version fragmentation, difficult upgrades of wrapped third-party dependencies, and variant sprawl.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Maintenance load is the recurring cost that regeneration avoids; platform headcount is the hidden line item.
insights.locator: Maintenance Is the Real Bill

insights.claim: A company-wide component library is effectively a product needing a roadmap, support load, deprecation policy and a team; if that team is starved, downstream projects end up patching around a library nobody owns.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Underfunded internal libraries decay within a couple of release cycles; a signal to cut or fund properly.
insights.locator: Maintenance Is the Real Bill

insights.claim: Tailwind's paid-component business was undercut by its own ubiquity in training data, because developers now prompt an AI for Tailwind components instead of visiting the documentation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Standardization that a vendor sells can become the thing that commoditizes its paid code; component-marketplace business models are exposed.
insights.quote: when developers need a Tailwind component, they don't visit the documentation. They prompt.
insights.locator: Regeneration Became Cheaper Than Reuse

insights.claim: The emerging model is reusable-to-regeneratable code: keep the specification and tests, regenerate the implementation on demand, and let tests let agents verify correctness independently.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Value migrates from code artifacts to specifications and test suites.
insights.locator: Regeneration Became Cheaper Than Reuse

insights.claim: Shared design systems, tokens, machine-readable guidelines and engineering principles together form the specification from which an agent generates components, replacing shipped component code as the centralized asset.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Invest in tokens and machine-readable guidelines rather than component packages.
insights.quote: The center of gravity moves from a shared code artifact to a shared set of constraints, which are still artifacts.
insights.locator: Centralize the Rules, Generate the Parts

insights.claim: Griffiths Waite uses the Figma MCP server to generate UI directly from Figma designs, finding it remarkably accurate, and adds custom skills to encode engineering best practices so output matches standards rather than model defaults.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Design-to-code via Figma MCP is in real production use; Figma's role as source of truth for agents is growing.
insights.locator: Centralize the Rules, Generate the Parts

insights.claim: Tokens are cheap to keep alive and are structured input that models handle well; teams already run one token definition through tools like Style Dictionary to emit CSS, iOS and Android values.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Token pipelines are the low-cost backbone for consistency across platforms.
insights.locator: Centralize the Rules, Generate the Parts

insights.claim: With regeneration, change control moves up the stack: versioning applies to skills, design systems, tokens and per-component instruction bundles rather than to shipped component code, and teams can regenerate only what changed.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Expect new tooling demand for versioning of specs and agent instruction bundles.
insights.locator: Change Control Moves Up the Stack

insights.claim: Regenerated UI must be verified rather than trusted, using visual-regression tools (Chromatic, Percy, Playwright), accessibility structure assertions, and computed-style checks that colors, spacing and type resolve to tokens.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Automated UI verification tooling becomes the gating layer as code generation commoditizes.
insights.locator: Centralize the Rules, Generate the Parts

insights.claim: Agents can compare a build against a Figma design through the MCP server and run screenshot comparison tests via the Playwright CLI to catch drift such as wrong shades or four-pixel padding errors that unit tests miss.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Agentic visual QA is practical today.
insights.locator: Centralize the Rules, Generate the Parts

insights.claim: A 2026 paper on software reuse in the generative AI era warns that blindly trusting generated code is akin to cargo cult development and that reuse of unproven assets can cause serious quality issues; the author reads this as a demand for testing, not a reason to avoid regeneration.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
entities: Software Reuse in the Generative AI Era
insights.so_what: Quality risk of AI code is real and must be priced into adoption.
insights.quote: conceptually not all that different from cargo cult development
insights.locator: Where a Shared Library Still Wins

themes.theme: Sea of sameness and opinionated systems

insights.claim: Models trained on the public web return the statistical middle of the training data for vague design prompts, producing homogeneous output (the same Tailwind blue, purple-to-cyan gradients and card grids from tools like Lovable, v0 and Base44).
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Undifferentiated AI-built UI is a commoditization risk for products relying on defaults.
insights.quote: A model "learns the center of that distribution, not its edges"
insights.locator: The Sea of Sameness Raises the Value of an Opinionated System

insights.claim: AI recommendations default toward Next.js, Tailwind and shadcn/ui, so shared tools, framework and component defaults reinforce uniform output.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Default-stack concentration entrenches incumbent frontend frameworks.
insights.locator: The Sea of Sameness Raises the Value of an Opinionated System

insights.claim: A 2026 Tilburg University meta-analysis found a small but statistically significant homogenization effect from AI use in co-creation, stronger in semantically constrained ideation tasks.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Homogenization is measurable, supporting a premium for differentiated, opinionated design.
insights.quote: small but statistically significant homogenization effect associated with AI use
insights.locator: The Sea of Sameness Raises the Value of an Opinionated System

insights.claim: A strong, opinionated design system (real type scale, color system, spacing rhythm, motion) is the lever that pulls model output off its average, so the design system matters more, not less, in a regeneration world.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Design-system quality becomes the differentiator when code generation is commoditized.
insights.locator: The Sea of Sameness Raises the Value of an Opinionated System

insights.claim: McKinsey's Business Value of Design study of 300 listed companies (2012-2017) found top-quartile MDI performers beat peers by 32 percentage points on revenue growth and 56 points on total returns to shareholders.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Supports a valuation link between design quality and returns for brand-facing products.
insights.locator: On Whether Sameness Really Matters

insights.claim: Sameness is not always a failure: Jakob's Law implies familiar layouts lower cognitive load, and for internal tools experience quality matters even where brand distinctiveness does not; much uniformity is lazy prompting and the longer trajectory may be generative UI tailored to each user.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Differentiate on brand-facing surfaces; accept convention for internal tools.
insights.locator: On Whether Sameness Really Matters

insights.claim: Accessibility is the strongest case for keeping curated shared components, since AI code generation tools do not excel at accessibility and generated UI is often inaccessible by default.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Accessibility-encoded component vendors retain a defensible niche.
insights.quote: AI code generating tools do not excel at accessibility
insights.locator: Where a Shared Library Still Wins

insights.claim: Well-known libraries give AI thousands of consistent examples as reference material, and configuring a trusted component is a smaller, safer diff to review than a two-thousand-line hand-rolled one.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Established libraries retain value as training and review anchors.
insights.locator: Where a Shared Library Still Wins

insights.claim: Recommended three-way split: regenerate high-volume low-risk surface (layout, typography, buttons, cards, simple forms), curate a few hard components (data grids, comboboxes, date pickers) as human-audited shared code, and keep design system, tokens, guidelines and tests central.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Practical allocation rule for platform teams deciding what to keep shared.
insights.locator: Verification Is Important

insights.claim: For organizations without a properly funded platform team, the shared library is the part that shrinks while the design system matters more, and this is not a loss worth mourning.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Expect leaner UI platform investment at mid-size firms; reallocate toward design systems and test suites.
insights.quote: The shared library is the part that shrinks.
insights.locator: So, Build One or Not?
